constraints.rationale: Both carry the rebuild's handling of the per-iteration framing: isIterationPrefixMessage exists only so the cold rebuild can tell the budget and working-list lines from the conversation, and restoreLoopFromRequest is the loop that drops that leading run before replaying the retained request. Changing what the predicate recognises changes what the rebuild seats.

The truncation self-heal budget is one fact split across files: handleLengthTruncation decides fail-versus-retry from retryCount, and publishedRetryOrdinal is where that count is read out of the durable PublishedRequestID so a replacement process spends the budget once. Neither side's behaviour can be understood without the other.

Both document the one classification ordering cannot make, a second delivery of the current request's answer. OutstandingRequest's doc says that is what the mark decides, and errResponseAlreadyApplied is the sentinel HandleModelResponse returns when the mark no longer names the response's request.

The create-versus-exists fence is split between them: HandleTask branches on ErrLoopAlreadyExists and calls attachContinuation, and attachContinuation's refusals and deferred flag drive HandleTask's continuation and deferral paths. Someone changing continuation admission must read both.

Gating a loop on a tool call is one workflow across two files: gateForApproval resolves the tool name and arguments and calls beginApprovalGate, which moves the live entity to awaiting_approval and clears the queue under the manager's lock. The ApprovalPendingEvent gateForApproval publishes is built from the state beginApprovalGate returns.

doc.go's 'A rebuild is not a reprieve' passage documents exactly the behaviour restoreDeadline implements: a loop rebuilt from its task keeps the record's StartedAt and TimeoutAt rather than the fresh deadline HandleTask would stamp. The method's own comment cites the same ruling in the same words.

deferredContinuationPrompt's doc names recoverEmptyContext as its one reader, and recoverEmptyContext re-injects the deferred turn from it after the birth prompt when the context has been emptied. The 'carried or not' predicate on the state side exists for that reader's situation.

publishIterationRequest's doc explains that the deferred-turn carrier bookkeeping does not live there but in TrackRequest, the call every request-minting site makes; TrackRequest's doc tells the same story from the other side, naming publishIterationRequest as where it used to live. Together they say which request carries a deferred turn.

QueuedToolCount exists to be 'the only honest bound on a drain loop', and synthesizeSkippedQueuedTools is that drain: it reads the count at entry, dequeues that many calls with synthetic results, and re-reads it to report growth. The bound's justification is written across both.

They are the two halves of the terminal-tool-less synthesis trigger in handleCompleteResponse: hasDecideToolCall says the trajectory shows no decide call, decideToolAvailable says the loop was granted decide (the gh#158 widening). Neither condition is meaningful for the SyntheticDecideRequest without the other.

Both are errors.New sentinels about a loop being 'terminal'. ErrLoopTerminal is task-intake admission, attachContinuation refusing to continue a settled loop, while errTerminalOwnedElsewhere is the carrier refusing to render a terminal record it does not own, part of the terminal-commit ownership protocol. Grouping them merges intake with terminal persistence.

Both are LoopManager 'timeout' setters with the same lock-and-store shape. SetTimeout stamps the loop's own deadline (TimeoutAt, read by IsTimedOut to fail the loop), whereas CacheRequestTimeout caches the TaskMessage's per-model-call timeout string that is copied onto every AgentRequest.Timeout; one is loop lifetime, the other a provider-call budget.

Both say 'truncat' and both produce a string. truncateToolResult caps an inbound tool result at ToolResultMaxBytes before it enters the context, while buildTruncationDiagnostic explains an OutcomeTruncated failure caused by the model's output hitting its length limit. Input-size capping and output-cutoff recovery are different responsibilities sharing one word.

Both are exported Build*Message(s) helpers on the handler side. BuildIterationBudgetMessage composes a system ChatMessage the model reads (prompt framing), while BuildFailureMessages serialises a LoopFailedEvent into a NATS PublishedMessage for agent.failed (terminal publication). 'Message' means a conversation turn in one and a wire envelope in the other.

Both are LoopManager Cache* setters called from HandleTask with identical lock shape. CacheTaskPrompt, despite its name, writes LoopEntity.TaskPrompt, a durable record field that rebuilds and terminal events read, while CacheMetadata fills a process-local, explicitly unpersisted map used to stamp outgoing tool calls. Record durability and runtime dispatch propagation are separate concerns.

Both are TrackRequest* methods called back-to-back at every request mint. TrackRequest records routing, the outstanding mark and the deferred-turn carrier, request-identity bookkeeping the response lane classifies against, whereas TrackRequestStart only stores a wall-clock for computeRequestDuration's trajectory timing. Identity and latency measurement are different responsibilities.

Adjacent Has* predicates with the same RLock-and-read shape. HasActiveLoopForTask is JetStream redelivery dedup by TaskID at task intake; HasPendingContinuation is the completion-time check that a deferred user turn still needs a carrier. One guards loop creation, the other decides whether a completing loop advances instead of settling.

Both carry 'Published'. PublishedMessage is the NATS envelope (subject, bytes, dedup MsgID) the component sends for any output, while SetPublishedRequest records invariant I1, the request the loop's durable record names, with ordering rules about when that name may be stamped. Wire publication and record authority are different subjects.

Both are LoopManager 'settle' mutators under the same lock. SettleRequest clears the outstanding-request mark and ends a carried deferral when a model response arrives (request lifecycle), whereas settleTerminal is the terminal owner's in-memory half of the terminal record write, clearing the approval gate and adopting a saved terminal. 'Settle' names a request in one and the loop's end in the other.

Both compute 'now is past a deadline' over the loop map. IsTimedOut reads the loop's own TimeoutAt and feeds failTimedOutLoop, while SnapshotExpiredApprovals reads PendingApproval.RequestedAt plus Timeout for the approval-timeout sweeper's auto-reject; doc.go describes the two deadlines as recovered separately. Loop lifetime and human-approval waiting are different responsibilities.
